theme: Levitical cities, cities of refuge; inheritance laws
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 35:1-36:13. The book ends with cities for the Levites, cities of refuge for those who kill accidentally, and a final ruling about inheritance. Read the cities of refuge slowly, as they are rich in meaning.
settingTheScene: The tribes are about to receive their land. The Levites, who have no tribal territory, are to be given forty-eight cities scattered among the others. Six of these are designated as cities of refuge, places where a person who has killed someone accidentally can flee and be safe. The book concludes with a follow-up to the case of the daughters of Zelophehad, since the tribes were concerned that their inheritance might pass from tribe to tribe.
observation: The Levites receive forty-eight cities with pasturelands (35:1-8).
Six are cities of refuge: three east of the Jordan, three west (35:9-15).
The one who kills by accident may flee to a city of refuge and be safe from “the avenger of blood” (35:11-12).
A murderer, however, may not take refuge, and must be put to death on the testimony of two or more witnesses (35:16-34).
The manslayer must stay in the city of refuge “until the death of the high priest” (35:25, 28).

“You shall not pollute the land in which you live, for blood pollutes the land, and no atonement can be made for the land for the blood that is shed in it, except by the blood of the one who shed it” (35:33).
“You shall not defile the land in which you live, in the midst of which I dwell, for I the LORD dwell in the midst of the people of Israel” (35:34).
The tribes are to keep their inheritance, and women who inherit must marry within their tribe (36:1-12).
interpretation:
The cities of refuge are one of the most beautiful provisions in the law. In the ancient world, if someone was killed, a relative was expected to take revenge. This cycle could consume whole families. God provides an alternative: places where a person who killed by accident could run and be safe until a fair trial. The law distinguishes between murder and manslaughter, and it protects the innocent while still taking life seriously.

The cities were spread out so that no one would be too far from one. The roads to them were kept in good repair, according to later tradition. They were open to everyone, Israelite or foreigner. The point is accessibility. A person in flight, with an avenger at his heels, could reach safety without delay.

The detail about the high priest is surprising. The manslayer must stay in the city until the high priest dies, and then he may go home. It seems arbitrary at first, but it contains a profound idea. The death of the high priest atones. His death is the end of the exile. It makes a way home for those who were under restraint.

The reason for the law is given in the last verses of chapter 35. Bloodshed pollutes the land, and the land cannot be cleansed except by the shedding of the murderer’s blood. God dwells in the land, so its purity is a matter of life and death. The same principle runs through the whole of Leviticus: where God dwells, sin must be dealt with.

The final chapter returns to a practical matter and ends on a note of order and obedience. The daughters of Zelophehad do as they were told. The book that began with a census ends with an inheritance. After forty years, the people are ready, at least in terms of structure, to enter the land.
connection: Hebrews 6:18 speaks of those “who have fled for refuge” to lay hold of the hope set before them, and Jesus is the one in whom we find refuge. He is also the high priest whose death sets the captives free (Hebrews 9:15). Paul says, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1). Jesus prayed on the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34).
application:
Think of Christ as your city of refuge, and run to him with whatever guilt you carry.

Consider whether you hold a grudge against someone, and whether you could extend mercy.

Thank God that the death of the great high priest has opened the way home.
prayerPrompts: Flee to Christ as your refuge, and tell him what you are running from.
Ask him to keep you from the cycle of vengeance.
Ask him to make you quick to show mercy.
